extracted.intended_audience: International Searching and Preliminary Examining Authorities (patent examiners) and applicants filing PCT international applications
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for International Searching and Preliminary Examining Authorities on conducting international searches and preliminary examinations under the PCT, covering unclear claims, excluded subject-matter, sequence listings, multiple dependent claims, and unity of invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search when description/claims fail Articles 5 and 6
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the description or claims fail to meet the requirements of Articles 5 and 6 to such an extent that it is impossible to examine claimed subject matter as to novelty, inventive step or industrial applicability, the examiner examines the claimed subject matter to the extent possible and establishes a written opinion reflecting the inadequate support or other deficiencies (see paragraph 17.35).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even after informal clarification by the applicant, objections on non-prior-art grounds remain in the written opinion because the claimed subject matter was and remains unclear absent such clarification. The written opinion should reflect inadequate support or other deficiencies for all or part of the claimed subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for clarification — defects in claim language
rubrics_metrics.description: A need for clarification may arise where defects in the claims cause difficulty in determining scope, for example, obscure, inconsistent, vague or ambiguous expressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These defects include cases where claim language is not clear even after taking the description and drawings into account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search strategy for claims containing alternatives with unclear realizations
rubrics_metrics.description: When claimed subject matter includes alternatives some of which are clear realizations and others unclear, the search examiner searches the clear realization; for unclear realizations the examiner determines the subject of search based on what might reasonably be expected to be claimed by amendment, taking into account the description, drawings and common general knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The written opinion and international preliminary examination report should establish opinions on novelty, inventive step and industrial applicability to the extent possible and explain why remainder could not be properly assessed. Examples: if claim is A+B+C+D and B is unclear, search to the extent possible; if an alternative is totally unclear so no reasonable subject can be determined, no search for that alternative is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent of search when part of claim is totally unclear
rubrics_metrics.description: If an element of a claim is totally unclear such that it is impossible to determine subject matter that may reasonably be expected to be claimed, no search is performed for that portion; search may proceed for the rest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: for (A1 or A2)+(B1 or B2), if A2 is totally unclear such that its reasonable scope cannot be determined, examiner need not search combinations involving A2 but should search combinations not involving the unclear alternative (e.g., A1+B1, A1+B2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Perpetual motion applications
rubrics_metrics.description: An international application pertaining to perpetual motion (perpetuum mobile) is not necessarily excluded from searching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ISA should endeavor to search such an application unless it is so unclear that Article 17(2)(a) (declaration of non-establishment of ISR) is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequence listing provision for meaningful search
rubrics_metrics.description: If an application contains nucleotide/amino acid sequences required to be in a sequence listing but the ISA does not have a compliant copy in an accepted language, the ISA requests provision of such a listing before establishing the search report/written opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If listing is not provided or not in required form/language, Authority makes a meaningful search or preliminary examination to the extent possible—for example, searching a named protein by name rather than by sequence. Note: sequences with fewer than ten specifically defined nucleotides or fewer than four specifically defined amino acids are not required to be included in a listing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declaration of non-establishment of international search report (Art.17(2)(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Where all claims constitute subject excluded from the search or where no meaningful search is possible for all claimed subject matter, a declaration of non-establishment of the ISR is issued on Form PCT/ISA/203 indicating the reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A written opinion is nonetheless established, but cannot address novelty and inventive step and may not address industrial applicability; detailed reasoning for non-addressing those questions may be referenced in the written opinion to the declaration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple dependent claims — formal rule (Rule 6.4(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Any dependent claim referring to more than one other claim (multiple dependent claim) shall refer to such claims in the alternative only and multiple dependent claims shall not serve as a basis for any other multiple dependent claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If national law of the Office acting as ISA does not allow multiple dependent claims drafted in a particular manner, the ISA may make an indication under Article 17(2)(b) only to the extent a meaningful search is not possible; such cases are noted in the written opinion. Examiner should consider not only the form of the claim itself but also the claims referred to in that claim to decide if it is multiple dependent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent claim containing references to multiple claims
rubrics_metrics.description: An independent claim may also contain a reference to another claim and, where it contains a reference to more than one other claim and serves as a basis for a multiple dependent claim, the ISA may indicate under Article 17(2)(b) if national law does not allow that manner of drafting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such an indication should only be made if and to the extent a meaningful search is not possible and is noted in the written opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplementary international search considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: The considerations in the chapter (e.g., on unclear claims, exclusions, unity) apply in general to supplementary international searches under Rule 45bis, with additional limitations possible by authorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See specified paragraphs (15.76–15.97) for supplementary search specifics; authorities may apply additional limitations (paragraphs 15.87 and 15.88).

rubrics_metrics.name: Excluded subject-matter: schemes, business methods, mental acts, games
rubrics_metrics.description: Key question is whether the claimed invention, viewed as a whole, is of abstract character or does not provide a practical application having a useful, concrete and tangible result; purely abstract schemes (e.g., learning schemes, crossword-solution methods, games as abstract entities, business organization schemes) may be excluded from search and examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If claimed subject matter specifies an apparatus or technical process for carrying out part of the scheme, the scheme plus apparatus/process must be searched and examined as a whole. For claims specifying computers or programs carrying out steps of a scheme, examine as a 'computer-related invention' if practical application exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excluded subject-matter: computer programs — practical application/technical character
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a computer program is excluded depends on whether the program has a practical application providing a useful, concrete and tangible result or whether it has technical character beyond a mere expression of an idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mere program listing not tangibly embodied on a computer-readable carrier is excluded. An executable program producing only an expression of an idea (e.g., mathematical theory) is excluded even if tangibly embodied. Conversely, a program tangibly embodied on a computer-readable carrier which when executed has a practical application should be searched and examined (e.g., computer program product). Data-processing operations implemented by program or by special circuits should be judged on technical character, not on implementation technology. Technical effect beyond normal interaction between program and computer indicates technical character (example: virtual extension of working memory providing practical effect).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of invention — single general inventive concept requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: An international application should relate to only one invention or, if more than one, inclusion is permitted only if all inventions are so linked as to form a single general inventive concept (Rule 13.1). Unity exists when there is a technical relationship among claimed inventions involving one or more of the same or corresponding special technical features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special technical features are those technical features that define a contribution which each of the inventions, considered as a whole, makes over the prior art. Determination is made on the contents of the claims as interpreted in light of the description and drawings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special technical features assessed with respect to novelty and inventive step
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a particular technical feature makes a 'contribution' over the prior art (and thus constitutes a special technical feature) is considered with respect to novelty and inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A document found in international search may establish lack of novelty or inventive step in a main claim, removing a technical relationship among claimed inventions and potentially leaving claims without a single general inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: A priori vs a posteriori lack of unity
rubrics_metrics.description: Lack of unity may be evident 'a priori' (before considering prior art) or 'a posteriori' (after considering prior art).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: independent claims A+X, A+Y, X+Y lack unity a priori; independent claims A+X and A+Y have unity a priori because A is common, but if A is known or obvious in the prior art, unity may be lacking a posteriori. Each case considered on merits; benefit of doubt to applicant; avoid narrow, literal or academic approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum reasoning methodology for assessing non-unitary subject-matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Authority may apply the 'minimum reasoning' methodology: ascertain common/corresponding matter, explain why this matter cannot provide a single general inventive concept due to lack of same/corresponding special technical features, and explain why there is no technical relationship among the inventions, if not apparent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysis may indicate non-common technical features and why claims are grouped, identify technical properties for each group demonstrated through features and explain differences; where appropriate (e.g., chemistry), explain structural or functional reasons claims are not similarly related. Examples provided in paragraphs 10.59E–10.59J.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not raise unity objection solely because of classification differences
rubrics_metrics.description: The Authority should not raise objection of lack of unity merely because the inventions claimed are classified in separate classification groups or merely for the purpose of restricting the international search to certain classification groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unity decision rests with ISA or IPEA and should be based on technical relationship and special technical features, not classification alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity consideration focused on independent claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity of invention has to be considered primarily in relation to the independent claims and not the dependent claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A dependent claim contains all features of one or more other claims and additional features. Note: a claim referring to another claim is not always a dependent claim (e.g., a claim to an apparatus 'for carrying out the process of Claim 1'). If independent claims avoid prior art and satisfy unity, dependent claims do not raise Rule 13 objections even if they contain further inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of unity a posteriori when independent claim does not avoid prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: If an independent claim does not avoid the prior art, the examiner must consider whether there remains an inventive link among the claims dependent on that claim; absence of such link may justify an objection of lack of unity a posteriori.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method is intended to be applied even before commencement of international search; initial unity determination based on assumption that claims avoid prior art may be reconsidered after search results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternatives within single claim and Rule 13.3 implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternative forms of an invention may be claimed either in multiple independent claims or in a single claim; the same unity criteria apply and lack of unity may exist within a single claim if it contains distinct embodiments not linked by a single general inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule 13.3 does not prevent an Authority from objecting to alternatives within a single claim on grounds such as clarity, conciseness of claims, or local claims fee systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination claims vs distinct embodiments (no unity objection normally)
rubrics_metrics.description: Objection of lack of unity does not normally arise if a number of individual elements are claimed in a single claim (a combination) even if elements seem unrelated when considered individually.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish combination of elements from distinct embodiments presented as alternatives; unity objections target the latter where no single general inventive concept links alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible combinations of different categories of claims (Rule 13.2 interpretation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Permitted combinations include (i) product + process specially adapted for manufacture + use of product; (ii) process + apparatus specifically designed for carrying out the process; (iii) product + process specially adapted for its manufacture + apparatus specifically designed for the process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A process is 'specially adapted' for manufacture if it inherently results in the product; an apparatus is 'specifically designed' if its contribution over prior art corresponds to the process's contribution. A single general inventive concept must link claims in various categories. Authorities should beware of proliferation of independent claims from combining provisions; accept such proliferation only exceptionally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'specially adapted' and 'specifically designed'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Specially adapted' means the claimed process inherently results in the claimed product and implies a technical relationship between product and process (but does not mean alternate processes are impossible). 'Specifically designed' means the apparatus/means' contribution over prior art corresponds to the process's contribution (but does not imply apparatus cannot be used for other processes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These definitions narrow when combinations qualify for unity under paragraph 10.12; they emphasize where the inventive emphasis resides (product vs process).

rubrics_metrics.name: Markush practice — unity for alternatives (chemical/non-chemical)
rubrics_metrics.description: A single claim defining alternatives ('Markush grouping') meets the unity requirement when the alternatives are of a similar nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For chemical compounds, 'similar nature' means: (A) all alternatives have a common property or activity, and (B) either (1) a common structure is present shared by all alternatives (a significant structural element or structurally distinctive portion essential to property/activity) or (2) all alternatives belong to a recognized class of chemical compounds in the art such that members are expected to behave similarly. Classification differences alone do not justify lack of unity. If at least one Markush alternative is not novel, unity should be reconsidered (though reconsideration does not necessarily mean an objection will be raised).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of intermediate and final products
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity is considered present between intermediate and final products where (A) the intermediate and final products have the same essential structural element (basic chemical structures the same or technically closely interrelated), and (B) they are technically interrelated meaning the final product is manufactured directly from the intermediate or via a small number of intermediates all containing the same essential structural element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unity may be recognized even when structures are unknown if sufficient evidence shows technical interrelation (e.g., intermediate incorporates essential element into final product). It is possible to accept different intermediates used in different processes for the final product provided they share the same essential structural element. Intermediates and final products must not be separated by an intermediate that is not new. For families of compounds, each intermediate compound must correspond to a compound claimed in the family of final products, though perfect congruence is not required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of examples to illustrate unity assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: The Guidelines provide numerous examples (Examples 1–39 and additional examples on lack of unity a posteriori) to illustrate applying unity principles in particular cases, including different claim categories, overlapping features, complementary forms, alternative forms, and dependent claims diverging from inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine the provided examples (paragraphs 10.21–10.59A etc.) for practical application of principles such as combinations, Markush practice, intermediate/final products, and minimum reasoning methodology.
